context:
In issue 10, "Hello in six tones" (greetings and small talk in the street; the six tones and the marks that write them), on a say screen.
The word on screen: Xin lỗi em. (Sorry. (to someone younger)) Note: xin lỗi plus the word for the person: em for someone younger.
This issue's new words: chào (hello; goodbye), biết (to know (a fact, or how to do something)), khỏe (well, healthy; strong), xin lỗi (sorry; excuse me), gặp (to meet (someone)).
This issue's sentence frame: Anh có ... không? Are you ...? Do you ...?
This issue's story: Six tones, five marks. Northern Vietnamese has six tones and writes five of them as marks; the level tone has none. The names are a gift to learners: each one is said in the tone it names, so ngang is level, huyền falls and sắc rises. Say the name and you hear the tone.
Issues played: 1 Phở and friends; 2 Big numbers and prices; 3 One to ten, properly; 4 People and family; 5 At the market; 6 At the table; 7 Getting around; 8 A numbers clinic; 9 Your turn to haggle.
Words the learner has met: gà (chicken), bò (beef; cow), cá (fish), trăm (hundred), nghìn (thousand), triệu (million), mươi (-ty, the tens (as in 20)), lăm (five, after the tens (as in 15 and 25)), linh (zero (for an empty tens place, as in 105)), rưỡi (and a half (after a unit)), tiền (money), bao nhiêu (how much, how many), đắt (expensive), rẻ (cheap), hơn (more than; -er (as in cheaper)), nữa (more, another), bốn (four), tám (eight), chín (nine (also: ripe, cooked)), ba (three), một (one), hai (two), năm (five (also: year)), sáu (six), bảy (seven), mười (ten), tên (name), tôi (I, me (neutral; safe with strangers)), anh (older brother; you (to a man a bit older)), chị (older sister; you (to a woman a bit older)), em (younger brother or sister; you (to someone younger)), cô (aunt; you (to a woman a bit younger than your parents)), chú (uncle; you (to a man a bit younger than your parents)), ông (grandfather; you (to an old man)), bạn (friend; you (to someone your own age)), bà (grandmother; you (to an old woman)), mua (to buy), quả (fruit; also the counting word for fruit), cam (orange (the fruit)), chuối (banana), cân (a kilo; also: scale, to weigh), thịt (meat), bớt (to take some off (a price); to reduce), hết (in total (of a bill); also: used up, sold out), mời (to invite; please (go ahead, have some)), cháu (grandchild, niece or nephew; I (to your parents' or grandparents' generation)), bát (bowl (a rice bowl)), đũa (chopsticks), canh (soup (a clear broth eaten with rice)), no (full (after eating)), vâng (yes (polite, to someone older)), uống (to drink), xe ôm (motorbike taxi), đâu (where), trái (left (the side)), gần (near, close by), rẽ (to turn (at a corner)), phải (right (the side)), nhăm (five after the tens, a casual spoken form of lăm (as in 25)), mốt (one at the end of 21, 31 ... 91 (11 stays mười một)), tư (four at the end of 24, 34 ... 94 (14 stays mười bốn)), chục (a set of ten things, as sellers count (ten eggs)), hàng (wares, goods; a shop or stall that sells them), được (OK, all right; can be done), lấy (to take; I'll have (at a stall or at the table)), trứng (egg).
Words they already knew: phở, cơm, bún, bánh mì, rau, nước, trà, cà phê, ngon, đồng.
Words still weak: nghìn, bao nhiêu, đắt, hơn, năm, tên, bạn, mua, chuối, gần, phải, tư, hàng, được, lấy.

turns.text: What am I supposed to say?
That phrase, **Xin lỗi em**, means "Sorry." **Xin lỗi** is "sorry" or "excuse me," and you use **em**, a word you know for a younger person, to address them.
the feedback that this page says say it but it doesn't say what to say.
And can you also ask the editors to add the back button because there's no way I can go back.
Thank you for that feedback! The editors read every conversation, so that's very helpful. The "say" prompt is likely just encouraging you to practice pronouncing **Xin lỗi em** and the tones.
